name: Al-'Ankabūt
revelation_details: Makkan (Late Makkan period, during intense persecution)
core_theme: The inevitability of trials (fitnah) for those who claim faith, the patience of believers, and the destruction of nations that relied on "spider-web" foundations.
name_origin:
The Surah takes its name from an evocative parable found in verse 41:

• "The example of those who take allies other than Allah is like that of the spider who takes a home. And indeed, the weakest of homes is the home of the spider, if they only knew."* (29:41)

Tafsir Insights on the Parable

• The "Weakest of Homes": In Tafsir, scholars note that the spider's house is the "weakest" because it offers no protection against the elements (heat, cold, rain) or predators. Similarly, a person who relies on idols, wealth, or status for spiritual or ultimate security is essentially homeless when the "storm" of the Hereafter or a major worldly trial arrives.
• The Gender of the Spider: The Qur'an uses the feminine form ittakhadhat (she took). Modern science confirms that it is the female spider that builds the web, and in many species, the "home" is a place of domestic strife where the female may kill the male - further symbolizing a home devoid of true peace or mercy.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: The surah opens by questioning whether people think they will be left alone just by saying they believe. Allah makes it clear that believers will be tested so that true faith is distinguished from false claims, just as gold is purified to separate it from dross.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: True faith is not a stagnant state but a proven quality that is only validated through the endurance of life's inevitable trials.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Those who commit evil cannot escape Allah's judgment. Whoever hopes to meet Allah should know that His appointed time will come. Striving in faith benefits the person himself, as Allah is entirely self-sufficient. Believers who do righteous deeds will have their sins removed and will be rewarded based on the best of their actions.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Every spiritual effort we make is an investment in our own souls, for God is in no need of our worship, yet He is most generous in rewarding it.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Kindness to parents is emphasized as a divine mandate, but if they pressure a person to associate partners with Allah or abandon faith, they must not be obeyed in that specific matter. All people will return to Allah, who will judge them, and sincere believers will be admitted among the righteous.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Our primary loyalty belongs to the Creator, and while we must remain kind to our parents, no human authority can supersede a divine command.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Some people claim belief, but when they face harm or social pressure for the sake of Allah, they treat that human persecution as if it were a punishment from Allah and abandon their faith. Yet, when victory and ease come, they claim to have been with the believers all along. Allah fully knows the secrets hidden in every heart.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Hypocrisy stems from a fear of worldly loss that outweighs the fear of God, leading to a fragmented soul that finds no peace.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Disbelievers invite others to follow their path and falsely promise to carry their sins on the Day of Judgment. Allah clarifies that they cannot carry anyone's burden except their own; instead, they will bear their own sins plus the additional weight of those they misled.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Influencing others toward falsehood does not divide one's guilt but multiplies it, as the leader shares in the consequences of the follower's actions.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Prophet Nuh lived among his people for 950 years calling them to the truth, yet they remained stubborn in their rejection. Eventually, the flood destroyed the wrongdoers, while Nuh and those with him were saved in the Ark as a lasting sign for all humanity.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Success in the sight of God is measured by steadfastness in the call to truth, regardless of the number of followers or the length of the struggle.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Ibrahim calls his people to worship Allah and be mindful of Him, pointing out the absurdity of idolatry. He explains that idols are powerless and cannot provide sustenance; therefore, people should seek provision from the Creator alone and show Him gratitude.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Dependence on the created is a form of poverty, while dependence on the Creator is the essence of true wealth and security.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: If people deny the message, they are reminded that earlier nations also denied their messengers and faced the consequences. The duty of the messenger is only to convey the message clearly. People are urged to reflect on how Allah originates creation and repeats it - a process that makes the resurrection of the dead logically certain.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Observation of the natural world is a gateway to understanding the spiritual reality of life after death.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: People are encouraged to travel the earth and observe the remains of past civilizations to see how creation began and ended. Allah, who has power over all things, will bring about the next creation. Those who lose hope in His mercy and deny the meeting with Him are those who face a painful punishment.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: A heart that loses hope in God's mercy has already begun to experience its own spiritual punishment.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Ibrahim's people responded to his logic with violence, trying to burn him alive, but Allah made the fire cool and saved him. Ibrahim then migrated for his Lord and was rewarded with a righteous lineage, including Ishaq and Ya'qub, ensuring that prophethood and scripture remained in his family.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: When an environment becomes hostile to one's faith, migration becomes the path to preserving the heart and finding God's expanded blessings.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Prophet Lut warned his people against unprecedented immoral acts and public crimes. They responded with defiance, mockingly daring him to bring God's punishment. Lut turned to Allah, praying for help against those who spread corruption.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Societies that normalize public indecency and mock divine boundaries eventually collapse under the weight of their own corruption.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Angels visited Ibrahim with news of a son and informed him of the impending destruction of Lut's town. Despite Ibrahim's concern, he was reassured that Lut and the believers would be saved, except for Lut's wife. The town was destroyed by a rain of stones, leaving ruins as a "clear sign" for people of understanding.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Divine justice is precise; it spares the innocent and identifies the guilty even within the same household.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Shu'ayb was sent to the people of Madyan, calling them to worship Allah and act with social justice. When they rejected him, a severe earthquake overtook them, leaving them lifeless in their homes as if they had never thrived there.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Economic injustice and the rejection of spiritual truth are a combined recipe for national ruin.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: The surah mentions the destruction of 'Ad, Thamud, and individual tyrants like Qarun, Pharaoh, and Haman. Despite their physical strength, wealth, and intellect, they were seized by various punishments: storms, blasts, and drowning. Allah emphasizes that He did not wrong them; they wronged themselves through arrogance.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: No amount of material advancement or intellectual prowess can shield a civilization that lacks a moral foundation.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Those who take protectors besides Allah are compared to a spider building a house. While the web is an intricate feat, it is the flimsiest of all shelters. This illustrates the extreme weakness of relying on anyone or anything other than Allah. Allah's creation is built on truth and wisdom, unlike the fragile illusions of men.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Relying on the ephemeral things of this world provides a false sense of security that vanishes the moment a real crisis arrives.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: The Prophet is commanded to recite the Qur'an and establish prayer, as prayer acts as a shield against immorality and wrongdoing. Believers are also told to argue with the People of the Book in the best possible manner, emphasizing their shared belief in the One God.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Prayer is the spiritual armor that protects the believer, and character is the bridge that connects them to others.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: The Qur'an confirms previous scriptures. Its divine origin is proven by the fact that the Prophet was unlettered and had never read or written books before. This leaves no room for doubters to claim he fabricated it. Despite this clear sign, some still demand physical miracles, ignoring the miracle of the Book itself.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: The greatest miracle is not a physical phenomenon but a message that transforms the human heart and intellect.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Allah is a sufficient witness between the Prophet and his critics. Those who reject the truth will face a sudden punishment. They arrogantly ask for the punishment to be hastened, unaware that Hell already surrounds those who disbelieve from every side.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: A delay in justice is not a denial of justice; it is merely an interval granted for people to reflect before the inevitable end.

verse_breakdowns.section_title: The Spacious Earth and Eternal Reward
verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Believers are encouraged to migrate if they are oppressed, for Allah's earth is vast and their worship should not be compromised. Every soul will taste death, and those who believe and do good will be rewarded with eternal, flowing gardens in Paradise as a reward for their patience.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: We are travelers in this world, and our true home is the one we build through our faith and patience today.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Allah provides for all creatures, even those that cannot store food. If people are asked who created the heavens and the earth or who sends down rain, they acknowledge it is Allah. Yet, despite this intellectual recognition, they still turn away from worshipping Him alone.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: It is a strange human contradiction to acknowledge God as the Provider while seeking help and guidance from those who provide nothing.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: This worldly life is described as temporary play and amusement, while the Hereafter is the "True Life." People show their true nature when they are in danger at sea, calling on Allah sincerely, only to return to polytheism once they are safe on land.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: We often find God in our tragedies only to forget Him in our triumphs, revealing that our "faith" is often just a reaction to fear.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Allah reminds the Makkans of the blessing of the secure sanctuary (the Haram) they enjoy while people all around them are being snatched away and killed. He asks how they can benefit from His security while denying His truth or inventing lies against Him.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Security and peace are blessings that demand gratitude and submission, not arrogance and denial.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: The surah concludes with a powerful promise: those who strive sincerely in Allah's cause will be guided to His many paths. Allah is always with the "Muhsinin" - those who pursue excellence and do good in all their affairs.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Sincere effort in seeking the truth is always met with divine light; the harder the struggle, the clearer the path becomes.

stories_in_surah.title: Deep Context of the Stories Mentioned
stories_in_surah.content:
The Long Patience of Nuh (Noah) - [Verses 14-15]

• The Detail: The Qur'an specifies that he stayed for 950 years.
• Tafsir Context: Ibn Kathir notes that despite this incredible length of time, only a small group believed. Every generation would warn the next not to listen to Nuh. This story served to tell the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him): "If your people reject you after 10 or 13 years, look at Nuh, who persisted for nearly a millennium without despairing."

Ibrahim (Abraham) and the Trial of Idolatry - [Verses 16-27]

• The Argument: Ibrahim's trial in this Surah focuses on his intellectual and spiritual debate. He told his people, "You only worship idols out of mutual affection in this world" (29:25), meaning their "faith" was just a social construct to keep their community together.
• The Miracle: When they threw him into the fire, Allah made it "cool and peaceful."
• The Hijrah (Migration): Ibrahim was the first to say, "I will emigrate to my Lord" (29:26). This provided the blueprint for the Sahaba (companions) who were about to migrate to Abyssinia and later Medina.

Lut (Lot) and the Trial of Public Vice - [Verses 28-35]

• The Specific Sin: The Surah highlights that they practiced their indecency "in their assemblies" (publicly).
• The Messengers: Angels first visited Ibrahim to give him news of a son (Ishaq) and told him they were going to destroy Lut's town. Ibrahim, being merciful, argued for them, but the angels replied that the decree was final.
• The Lesson: Lut's trial was the loneliness of being the only righteous household in an entire city of vice.

The Destruction of the Materialists: 'Ad, Thamud, and Qarun - [Verses 38-40]

• 'Ad and Thamud: They were "keen-sighted" and technologically advanced. They carved homes into mountains (Thamud) and built pillars ('Ad). Their trial was intellectual arrogance - they thought their science and engineering made them invincible.
• Qarun (Korah): A relative of Musa (Moses) who turned against him. He was so wealthy that the keys to his treasure rooms were a burden for a group of strong men to carry.
• The End: He claimed his wealth was due to "knowledge I possess." Because he relied on his wealth (a spider's web), Allah caused the earth to swallow him and his home.

deep_dives.title: The Central Theme: The Necessity of Trials
deep_dives.content:
The Surah opens with a fundamental question: "Do people think that they will be left alone because they say: 'We believe,' and will not be tested?" (29:2).

According to authentic Hadith, this was revealed regarding the companions in Makkah who were being brutally tortured. It taught them that Iman (faith) is a claim that must be proven through the "fire" of hardship, just as gold is purified by fire.

deep_dives.title: Historical Context (The Fitnah of the Parents)
deep_dives.content:
Verse 8 mentions the trial of parents who force their children into shirk.

• Authentic Context: Asbab al-Nuzul (reasons for revelation) cite the story of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. When he converted, his mother went on a hunger strike, saying, "I will not eat or drink until you disbelieve in Muhammad." Sa'd loved his mother but said, "Even if you had a hundred souls and they left you one by one, I would not leave my religion."
• The Balance: The verse was revealed to show that while you must be "kind and good" to parents, you cannot obey them in matters that contradict God's commands.

deep_dives.title: Summary Table of Contextual Lessons
deep_dives.content:
• Subject: The Test — Verse: 2 — Context/Source: Persecution in Makkah — Primary Lesson: Faith requires evidence of patience.
• Subject: Nuh — Verse: 14 — Context/Source: 950 years of Da'wah — Primary Lesson: Success is measured by sincerity, not numbers.
• Subject: Ibrahim — Verse: 24 — Context/Source: The Great Fire — Primary Lesson: God is the only protector when all people turn away.
• Subject: Qarun — Verse: 39 — Context/Source: Musa's arrogant cousin — Primary Lesson: Wealth is a test, not a sign of God's favor.
• Subject: The Spider — Verse: 41 — Context/Source: Parable of the Web — Primary Lesson: Worldly power is fragile and temporary.

Through these stories, Surah Al-Ankabut bridges the gap between the suffering of the early Muslims and the triumphs of the Prophets, proving that the "Spider's Web" of the oppressors will eventually fall.
